user_query: Why does the paper claim that the LINE inference algorithm is quite scalable, and what implementation choices support that claim?
llm_response: The paper calls the LINE inference algorithm quite scalable because its per-iteration cost is linear in the number of observed edges and it avoids expensive global operations such as full matrix factorization or repeated passes over all possible node pairs. In practice, the algorithm only needs local computations on sampled edges and their negative samples, so it can be trained efficiently even on very large graphs. The implementation choices that support this claim include using stochastic gradient descent with edge sampling, negative sampling to approximate the normalization term, asynchronous or parallel updates to the embeddings, and a simple embedding lookup/update structure that keeps memory and computation overhead low. Together, these choices make the method suitable for large-scale networks and allow it to scale roughly linearly with graph size in the number of edges processed.
llm_confidence_reasoning: This is consistent with the standard LINE paper description and its implementation strategy, though exact wording and some details may vary by version or summary.
